lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Greet someone at any hour, and meet the capital letter that every German noun wears.
lessons.explanation: German greetings follow the hour rather than the person: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend. Hallo ignores the clock and is what you will actually hear most in a doorway or a shop. The habit worth starting on day one is that every German noun takes a capital letter wherever it sits in a sentence, which is why Kaffee and Nation look like names.
lessons.culturalNote: German capitalizes every noun — Nation, Kaffee. The capital letter is part of the spelling.

exercises.prompt: This is the first word out of your mouth in a Berlin bakery. What does «Hallo» mean?
exercises.explanation: Hallo is hello. German keeps one greeting for every hour of the day, which is why this is the one to learn cold.

exercises.prompt: You step into a bakery at nine in the morning. Say the word that greets the baker before anything else.
exercises.explanation: Say it before you look. One word is all this needs.

exercises.prompt: German gives a capital letter to every noun. Which pair is capitalised for that reason?
exercises.explanation: Kaffee and Nation are nouns, so they keep their capital anywhere in the sentence. Danke, ja, nein and hallo are not nouns and stay lowercase.

exercises.prompt: Complete the word you say as you come through the door: ___
exercises.explanation: Hallo comes before the request, not after it.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. How many times does somebody say no?
exercises.passage:
— Hallo!
— Hallo.
— Kaffee?
— Ja, danke.
— Noch ein Kaffee?
— Nein, danke.
exercises.explanation: The second offer is refused with nein. The first is accepted with ja.

exercises.prompt: Type the greeting and the thanks you hear, in that order.
exercises.explanation: Hallo opens it and danke closes it.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Greet someone in Spanish, and meet the opening question mark that Spanish puts in front.
lessons.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.
lessons.culturalNote: Hola works everywhere, all day. Gracias answers everything from gifts to directions.

exercises.prompt: A friend says this to you in Madrid before anything else is said. What does «Hola» mean?
exercises.explanation: Hola needs no clock. Morning, afternoon or night, this is the greeting that works.

exercises.prompt: Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark and closes it with an ordinary one. Which of these is asking something?
exercises.explanation: Only the first line is a question: it carries the upside-down opening mark and the closing one. The other two are statements and need neither.

exercises.prompt: You meet a friend in Madrid. Greet them before anything else is said.
exercises.explanation: One word is all this needs. Say it aloud before you check.

exercises.prompt: Complete the greeting you give a friend: ___
exercises.explanation: Hola comes first; the rest of the sentence waits.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange and count the questions in it.
exercises.explanation: Two of the lines open with the upside-down mark. The other four are statements.

exercises.prompt: Write down both words. The second one is a thank you.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Greet someone in Portuguese, and learn why thanks changes shape depending on who is speaking.
lessons.explanation: Portuguese greets by the hour, but one word here behaves differently from every language around it: obrigado is not fixed. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the person speaking rather than the person being thanked. Get that right on day one and you will sound like yourself rather than like a phrasebook.
lessons.culturalNote: Olá works everywhere, all day. Obrigado ends in -o when men say it and -a (obrigada) when women say it.

exercises.prompt: It opens every conversation in Lisbon. What does «Olá» mean?
exercises.explanation: Olá is hello, and unlike the time of day it never changes. One word covers the whole morning and the whole night.

exercises.prompt: You meet a neighbour in Lisbon. Greet them before anything else is said.
exercises.explanation: Say it once out loud, then look.

exercises.prompt: A woman is the one speaking, and she is thanking a colleague. Which form is hers?
exercises.explanation: Obrigada agrees with the woman speaking. Obrigado is what a man says, and obrigados is for a group.
This is the masculine speaker form. A woman says obrigada, and both mean the same thing to the person hearing them.

exercises.prompt: Complete the greeting you say as you arrive: ___
exercises.explanation: Olá comes before the request, not after it.

exercises.prompt: Write the two words the woman says, in the order she says them.
exercises.explanation: She is a woman thanking someone, so she says obrigada rather than obrigado.
